subject: music
promptStrong: Give me an exam-style {board} {level} {subject} question on {lo}, then mark my answer against the mark scheme.
promptWeak: Explain {lo} for {board} {level} {subject} simply, with a clear example and the most common mistake students make.

questions.q: Which Italian dynamic marking means 'loud'?
questions.explain: Forte (f) instructs the performer to play loudly, whereas piano (p) means soft.

questions.q: What is the term for a short rhythmic or melodic pattern repeated persistently throughout a passage?
questions.explain: An ostinato is a repeated pattern used to give music unity and drive.

questions.q: In CCEA GCSE Music Component 2, one of the two compositions must be written in response to what?
options: A set work studied in class
A poem chosen by the teacher
A recording of a live performance
questions.explain: CCEA releases stimuli each year and candidates compose one piece responding to a chosen stimulus.

questions.q: What defines the 'free composition' in CCEA GCSE Music Component 2?
options: It is composed in a style or genre of the candidate's own choice
It must be written for solo piano only
It must respond to a CCEA stimulus
It must be in strict four-part harmony
questions.explain: The free composition lets candidates choose their own style, genre and instrumentation.

questions.q: Which cadence uses the chord progression V–I?
questions.explain: A perfect cadence moves from the dominant (V) to the tonic (I), giving a finished sound.

questions.q: What does the term 'diminuendo' instruct a performer to do?
questions.explain: A diminuendo is a gradual decrease in volume, the opposite of a crescendo.

questions.q: A texture consisting of a single, unaccompanied melodic line is described as:
questions.explain: Monophonic texture has only one melodic line with no accompaniment.

questions.q: What proportion of the overall CCEA GCSE Music qualification is Component 2 (Composing) worth?
questions.explain: Composing is weighted at 30%, with Performing and Listening each carrying 35%.

questions.q: Which musical element refers to the characteristic tone colour or quality of a sound?
questions.explain: Timbre (tone colour) is what makes a flute sound different from a trumpet playing the same note.

questions.q: Which statement best describes homophonic texture?
options: A melody supported by chordal accompaniment
A single melody with no accompaniment
Two performers echoing each other in turn
questions.explain: Homophonic texture combines a clear main melody with harmonic (chordal) accompaniment.

questions.q: What is a melodic 'sequence'?
options: Repetition of a melodic idea at a higher or lower pitch
A repeated bass note held under changing harmony
questions.explain: A sequence repeats a melodic pattern starting on a different pitch, developing the material.

questions.q: Ternary form is best represented by which structural pattern?
questions.explain: Ternary form has three sections where the opening A section returns after a contrasting B section.

questions.q: Why is planning a clear structure important in a free composition?
options: It gives the music shape, coherence and a sense of direction
It guarantees the piece will be in a major key
It removes the need to use musical elements
It makes the piece automatically longer
questions.explain: A planned structure helps ideas develop logically and holds the listener's interest.

questions.q: What is the main purpose of a stimulus in a composition task?
options: To provide a starting point or idea that inspires the music
To dictate the exact notes that must be used
To restrict the piece to one instrument
To replace the need for a structure
questions.explain: A stimulus offers an initial idea or mood that the composer interprets and develops musically.

questions.q: Syncopation is best described as:
options: Placing accents on normally weak beats or off-beats
Repeating a bass note underneath the harmony
questions.explain: Syncopation stresses off-beats or weak beats, creating rhythmic interest and drive.

questions.q: What does 'modulation' mean in a composition?
options: Changing from one key to another
questions.explain: Modulation is a shift from one key to another, often used to add variety or contrast.

questions.q: A composer wants a flowing, smooth and connected melody line. Which articulation should be marked?
questions.explain: Legato tells the performer to play notes smoothly and connected.

questions.q: To build tension and drive towards a climax, which combination of elements would be most effective?
options: A crescendo with rising pitch and an accelerando
A diminuendo with falling pitch and a rallentando
Soft dynamics, a slow tempo and a thin texture
A single sustained pedal note held quietly
questions.explain: Increasing volume, pitch and speed together intensifies the music towards a climax.

questions.q: A candidate composing a free piece for solo piano wants a contrasting middle section. Which approach best achieves this?
options: Change the key and dynamics to create a contrasting section
Repeat the opening material exactly with no changes
Remove all rhythm from the middle section
Play the same phrase continuously at one dynamic
questions.explain: Altering tonality and dynamics provides clear contrast, as in the B section of ternary form.

questions.q: Responding to a stimulus depicting a 'storm', which set of musical choices best reflects it?
options: Loud dynamics, a fast tempo, dissonant harmony and a busy texture
Soft dynamics, a slow tempo and a sparse, gentle melody
A single quiet legato line with no accompaniment
A steady, unchanging chord held throughout at piano
questions.explain: Powerful dynamics, rapid tempo, dissonance and thick texture musically suggest the drama of a storm.

specSource: CCEA GCSE Music (2017) specification; Component 2: Composing
